source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for MoE. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Assume a fixed MoE checkpoint, fixed precision, fixed number of devices, and a quality-matched dense or alternate-routing comparator. Use a small factorial experiment with prompt length, decode output length, and concurrency varied while holding tokenizer, sampling, software, and hardware constant. Mechanism: instrument the router's top-k assignment, all-to-all dispatch to expert owners, expert execution, and gather/combine separately. Run warm-up plus repeated trials for prefill and decode, recording median and p95/p99 latency, tokens/s, GPU memory, communication time, expert-load imbalance, overflow/fallback rate, and output-quality checks. Boundary: an active-FLOP reduction need not improve end-to-end decode when batches are small, routing is skewed, KV memory is tight, or the interconnect saturates; do not generalize beyond the tested workload and capacity policy.
risks: A throughput gain can come from changed quality, overflow, or an unmatched baseline.
Expert skew and communication contention can dominate the small experiment and vary with workload.
evidence_required: Exact checkpoint, comparator, precision, topology, router top-k, capacity/overflow policy, prompt/output lengths, concurrency, and software versions.
Repeated phase-specific latency, throughput, memory, dispatch/combine time, expert histograms, overflow/errors, and quality measurements.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for MoE. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Start with one fixed model and a quality-matched baseline; state that the goal is serving behavior, not a universal cost claim. Sweep only two factors initially—concurrency and prompt length—with fixed generated length, precision, placement, and sampling. Mechanism: for each batch, record top-k router assignments, token dispatch across ranks, expert compute, and result combine, so communication and imbalance are not hidden inside a single timer. After warm-up, repeat each cell and report prefill and decode median/p95 latency, throughput, memory high-water mark, expert occupancy, queueing, overflow/fallback, and correctness or quality. Boundary: conclusions apply only to the tested sequence lengths and load; at another concurrency or with hot experts, capacity and all-to-all contention may reverse the result.
risks: Changing generated length or quality target confounds comparisons.
Router imbalance and overflow can change both latency and outputs.
evidence_required: Model and baseline identity, quality criterion, device mapping, precision, fixed lengths, concurrency, top-k, and overflow behavior.
Per-cell repetitions with prefill/decode timing, communication, memory, expert loads, tails, failures, throughput, and quality.

source_user: Design a small controlled experiment for MoE. Case variant 4: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Define a minimal A/B test: the same checkpoint and prompts run with the normal MoE router and a controlled routing or placement variant, with precision, devices, batch policy, and sampling fixed. Use matched prompt and output lengths and enough warm-up to exclude startup. Mechanism: capture the router assignment, scatter/all-to-all transfer, expert kernels, and gather/combine as separate spans; correlate them with expert token counts. Measure prefill and decode latency percentiles, tokens/s, memory, network utilization, queueing, overflow/dropped-token or fallback counts, and output quality. Boundary: a result from prefill at high batch cannot be applied to autoregressive decode at low batch, where synchronization and communication may dominate.
risks: A routing variant may alter model quality and is not a fair performance comparison without a quality check.
Phase mixing can hide decode tail latency and memory pressure.
evidence_required: Router and placement definitions, checkpoint, quality test, fixed workload, precision, topology, batching, and capacity limits.
Separate phase traces, communication and kernel times, expert balance, memory, latency tails, throughput, overflow, and quality.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating MoE. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Runbook: first record checkpoint, precision, device topology, router top-k, capacity factor, overflow/fallback policy, workload lengths, concurrency, and software versions. Reproduce the issue after warm-up and separate prefill from decode. Inspect router histograms, per-expert token counts, dispatch/all-to-all and combine spans, expert kernel time, KV-cache and other memory high-water marks, queueing, and p95/p99 latency. Compare only with the same quality target and matched workload. Mechanism: tokens are assigned to expert owners, transferred, processed, then gathered and combined. Boundary: “few active experts” does not guarantee lower serving latency when expert skew, capacity overflow, small decode batches, or network saturation dominates; preserve logs and stop broad claims until those factors are measured.
risks: Missing router or overflow telemetry makes root-cause attribution speculative.
A fallback or dropped-token policy can trade quality for apparent speed.
evidence_required: Configuration and topology snapshot plus representative prompts and load.
Phase traces, expert-load distribution, communication, memory, queueing, latency percentiles, failures, and quality checks.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating MoE. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Runbook: pin the model and runtime, capture precision, placement, top-k, capacity and overflow settings, and describe prompt/output lengths and arrival load. Reproduce with warm-up, then profile prefill and decode separately. Check router balance and hot experts, token dispatch and gather/combine time, expert execution, synchronization, KV-cache memory, queueing, and p50/p95/p99 latency. Validate output quality before comparing throughput. Mechanism: top-k routing scatters each token's activation to selected expert ranks and combines their returned outputs. Boundary: measurements at one batch size or phase do not establish general behavior; low-concurrency decode or a saturated link can erase an MoE compute advantage.
risks: Unmatched load or phase definitions can misdiagnose a communication problem.
Capacity limits may cause overflow, fallback, or quality regressions.
evidence_required: Reproducible configuration, representative workload, matched comparator, and quality criterion.
Expert histograms, dispatch/combine and synchronization traces, memory, queueing, phase latency, throughput, errors, and quality.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating MoE. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Runbook: establish a reproducible baseline and document checkpoint, precision, topology, routing, capacity factor, overflow policy, batch/concurrency, and sequence lengths. Warm up, then collect separate prefill/decode traces. Look for token-count skew by expert, all-to-all/dispatch and combine stalls, expert kernel utilization, synchronization, KV-cache pressure, queueing, and latency tails. Mechanism: the router selects top-k experts, dispatches activations to their owners, runs them, and combines the outputs. Boundary: resident memory includes model weights and potentially all experts even when active compute is sparse; do not infer memory safety or latency from active FLOPs alone. Escalate only with repeated measurements and quality/failure checks.
risks: Sparse active compute can be confused with sparse resident memory.
Expert skew and cache pressure can create tail failures not visible in averages.
evidence_required: Memory accounting by weights, activations, KV cache, buffers, and communication; plus exact routing and capacity settings.
Repeated phase-level traces, expert balance, latency percentiles, throughput, OOM/overflow/fallback counts, and quality.

source_user: Write a concise runbook entry for an engineer investigating MoE. Case variant 5: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Mixture-of-Experts routes tokens to selected experts, reducing active compute per token but introducing routing, capacity, and all-to-all concerns.
corrected_answer: Runbook: freeze configuration and note model, precision, expert placement, top-k, capacity/overflow behavior, workload distribution, and runtime. Reproduce after warm-up and split prompt prefill from token-by-token decode. Instrument router assignments, per-expert occupancy, dispatch/all-to-all, expert kernels, combine, synchronization, KV-cache/memory, queueing, and p95/p99 latency; compare quality and failures with a matched baseline. Mechanism: selected token activations are sent to expert owners and their results are gathered and combined. Boundary: an MoE benefit is workload- and topology-dependent; skewed routing, small decode batches, limited capacity, or interconnect contention may make it slower or less reliable. Keep the claim limited to measured conditions.
risks: Averaging away tail latency or failures can hide operational risk.
Changing overflow behavior may improve speed while changing outputs.
evidence_required: Configuration, topology, workload/load range, matched baseline, and quality target.
Per-phase repeated latency, throughput, memory, communication, expert balance, queueing, overflow/failures, and quality.

source_user: Define quantization and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 1: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer: Quantization represents weights, activations, or KV-cache values with fewer bits or a constrained numeric format than the original representation, usually using a scale (and sometimes zero-point or groupwise parameters) to map values. Mechanism: an int8 or int4 weight is dequantized or consumed by a supported low-precision kernel during matrix multiplication, reducing storage and potentially memory bandwidth. This matters because it can increase feasible model or batch size and improve serving efficiency, but it is not guaranteed. Boundary: benefits require hardware/runtime kernel support and may disappear when dequantization or unsupported operations dominate; calibration and outlier handling can also change accuracy. Measure memory, phase latency, throughput, errors, and quality against the same workload and target.
risks: Lower bit width can introduce accuracy or numerical-stability regressions.
Reported speedups may reflect a different kernel, batch, or quality target rather than quantization alone.
evidence_required: Quantized tensors, bit width, scale/calibration method, outlier policy, kernel/runtime and hardware support.
Matched quality tests plus memory, dequantization/kernel breakdown, prefill/decode latency, throughput, and failures.

source_user: Define quantization and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer: Quantization maps higher-precision values to a smaller numeric representation, such as per-tensor, per-channel, or groupwise int8/int4 values with associated scales. Mechanism: a low-precision GEMM can load fewer bytes per weight and accumulate in a wider type, lowering weight-memory traffic while retaining a defined dequantization or scaling rule. It matters for fitting large models, increasing batch capacity, or reducing bandwidth pressure. Boundary: fewer bits alone do not ensure lower latency—if the device lacks a native kernel, tensors are repeatedly converted, or activations/KV cache remain unquantized, overhead may dominate. Evaluate a fixed model and workload for memory, latency, throughput, and task quality.
risks: Scale granularity and calibration data affect accuracy and overhead.
Mixed precision can make nominal model bit width misleading for total memory.
evidence_required: Representation and scale granularity, accumulation type, calibration data, supported kernels, and which tensors are quantized.
End-to-end and kernel-level memory/latency measurements, throughput, batch capacity, and quality/error checks.

source_user: Define quantization and explain one reason it matters in LLM infrastructure. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Quantization reduces representation precision and often memory traffic, but accuracy, kernel support, calibration, and outlier handling must be measured.
corrected_answer: Quantization is the deliberate conversion of model values from a higher-precision format to a lower-bit or otherwise restricted format, using scales and possibly zero-points to limit reconstruction error. Mechanism: groupwise int4 weights are loaded with group scales and multiplied by activations in a kernel that accumulates in higher precision; the smaller weights can reduce bandwidth and resident memory. It matters because memory capacity and bandwidth often constrain LLM serving. Boundary: the conclusion is conditional on supported kernels and calibration: outliers, conversion overhead, or quantized activations/KV-cache behavior may cause quality loss or erase the gain. Compare against an unquantized reference with identical prompts, lengths, load, hardware, and quality checks, and report uncertainty.
risks: Quantization error can disproportionately affect sensitive layers or long-context behavior.
Memory savings may be overstated if scales, metadata, buffers, or unquantized tensors are omitted.
evidence_required: Bit format, scale scheme, metadata, calibration set, outlier handling, tensor coverage, and kernel/hardware support.
Full memory accounting, kernel and end-to-end phase timings, throughput, quality metrics, long-context checks, and failure logs.
